findings.claim: TNUoS (transmission network charges) is set by NESO under its licence and the CUSC. Total revenue recovered is rising, and a large 'demand residual' element is passed through to demand customers. NESO forecasts further increases for 2027/28.
findings.evidence: NESO webinar slides (May 2026), 'Initial TNUoS Tariffs for 2027/28': NESO is forecasting and setting TNUoS "to recover around £9bn of revenue per year from generators and demand; in addition to BSUoS". NESO has a licence and CUSC obligation to publish quarterly TNUoS forecasts and an annual Five-Year View. Final 2027/28 tariffs are due by 31 January 2027 and take effect from 1 April 2027. Total TNUoS revenue is forecast at £9.11bn for 2027/28, up £1.50bn on the 2026/27 final tariffs, driven mainly by onshore transmission owner allowed revenues (up £1.58bn). Demand revenue is forecast at £7.73bn, up £1.35bn. The demand residual tariff is forecast to be 21% higher than 2026/27, and demand residual charges are expressed as £/day by charging band. The average half-hourly (HH) demand tariff is forecast at £3.48/kW (up £0.69/kW) and the average non-half-hourly (NHH) tariff at 0.48p/kWh (up 0.10p/kWh). TNUoS on the average consumer electricity bill is forecast at £96.85, up £13.61. The slides also say substantial change to the charging methodology (the Reform of National Pricing programme) is expected but is not included in the forecast.
findings.limitations: These are initial forecasts (May 2026), not final tariffs, and are written for industry participants. The slides give no explanation of how suppliers pass these charges into a business contract. The £96.85 figure refers to the average consumer bill, not a business bill. No Ofgem page was read for DUoS. The page shows no formal date beyond 'May 2026'.

findings.claim: BSUoS (balancing services charges) is set and published by NESO as a fixed tariff in advance, and since 1 April 2023 it has been recovered only from final demand, including suppliers.
findings.evidence: NESO BSUoS page: "The BSUoS charge recovers the cost of day-to-day operation including the cost of balancing the electricity transmission system." It applies to final demand sites, suppliers and directly-connected transmission demand, and not to generators, DNOs, embedded generators or interconnectors, with exemptions. CMP308 and CMP361 came into effect on 1 April 2023: CMP308 defined that BSUoS charges are recovered solely from final demand, and CMP361 introduced an ex-ante fixed BSUoS tariff. Fixed tariffs 7 and 8 for 2026/27 were published on 29 December 2025.
findings.limitations: The page does not give the tariff level and does not say how a supplier passes BSUoS on to business contracts. The extract shows no single publication date for the page.

findings.claim: Renewables Obligation (RO): an obligation on suppliers, not a charge set directly on business customers. It is closed to new capacity but still operates.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: the RO closed to all new generating capacity on 1 April 2017. It places an annual obligation on electricity suppliers to present ROCs per MWh supplied in each obligation period (1 April – 31 March), or to pay into a buy-out fund, or to do a combination. Ofgem accredits stations, issues and revokes ROCs, receives buy-out payments and redistributes the funds. The page says nothing about how suppliers recover this cost from customers.
findings.limitations: The Ofgem page describes the scheme mechanics only. It does not say that the cost is passed to non-domestic customers, nor give the obligation level or the cost per MWh. The same applies to the Feed-in Tariff, CfD levy and capacity market: no official page covering them was read, so this finding should not be treated as corroboration of the GLCG list for those items. The page shows no date.

findings.claim: Comparison with the GLCG breakdown from earlier research: the official sources read partly corroborate it, since NESO describes TNUoS and BSUoS as network and system charges set centrally. They do not corroborate its claim that these costs are charged at actual cost under pass-through contracts, or its list of levies.
findings.evidence: GLCG lists TNUoS/DUoS, BSUoS, CCL and RO/FiT as bill line items, bundled into the rate in fully fixed contracts and passed through at actual cost in pass-through contracts. The NESO pages confirm that TNUoS and BSUoS are set by NESO, that BSUoS is recovered from final demand and suppliers via a fixed tariff, and that TNUoS revenue is rising. Ofgem confirms the RO places the obligation on suppliers. GOV.UK (read in an earlier task) sets CCL rates. None of these official pages says how a supplier passes the charges through in a particular contract type.
findings.limitations: This is a synthesis across sources. None of the official pages addresses fixed versus pass-through contract treatment, so that part of GLCG's account remains from a commercial source only.

findings.claim: Ofgem's business switching guidance: when you can switch depends on the contract type. Fixed-rate contracts usually cannot be left early without an exit fee or an agreed termination clause, though a pre-expiry 'switching window' may allow a fee-free switch. Variable, evergreen, out-of-contract and deemed customers can switch at any time. The existing supplier may object to a switch, for example if you owe it money.
findings.evidence: Ofgem: for fixed-rate contracts, "Most suppliers will not let you switch before the end of your contract unless you have already agreed a termination clause or pay an exit fee." Fixed-rate contracts include a 'switching window', a set period to renew or say you intend to leave, which opens a few months before the end. You can sometimes switch in that window without a fee. With a variable-rate contract, including a rolling or 'evergreen' contract, out-of-contract rates or a deemed-rate contract, "you can switch to a new supplier at any time". You must give the new supplier your annual consumption and meter details before signing. "Your existing supplier may object to your switch, for example if you owe them money. If this happens, get in touch with them as soon as possible." Customers moving premises are responsible for energy used before a new contract starts and may be put on a deemed-rate contract. Citizens Advice (earlier source) also notes a switch to the new supplier completes within 5 working days.
findings.limitations: The Ofgem page lists only a debt objection as an example and does not set out the full list of permitted objection grounds, nor give the non-domestic switching timeline. The 5-working-day figure comes from Citizens Advice. The Ofgem page shows no date, and no licence condition numbers are given on it.

findings.claim: Termination-notice rules for microbusinesses have changed in two steps. Since 30 April 2015 the maximum notice was 30 days. Since 1 October 2022 suppliers cannot require microbusinesses to give notice to switch, except on evergreen contracts.
findings.evidence: Ofgem factsheet (29 July 2015): since 30 April 2015 the maximum notice period for terminating a micro-business contract was reduced from 90 to 30 days. Suppliers must include current prices, new prices and annual consumption on renewal letters for fixed-term contracts. They must take all reasonable steps to acknowledge termination notice within five working days of receipt. CMS law-firm summary of Ofgem's Microbusiness Strategic Review decision (28 March 2022): the decision prohibited suppliers from requiring microbusinesses to give prior notice of termination, except for Evergreen Contracts, in force from 1 October 2022. The rationale was to ease switching. Retaining the evergreen exemption typically lets suppliers offer non-fixed-term options at lower cost than deemed or out-of-contract rates. Ofgem's current business-contract guidance (read earlier) still states the 30-day limit and 5-working-day acknowledgement as applying to evergreen contracts only.
findings.limitations: The CMS page is a law-firm summary of the Ofgem decision, not the decision itself. The 2015 factsheet is dated and pre-dates the 2022 change, so the 2022 decision supersedes it for fixed-term contracts.

findings.claim: Licence references and related 2022 changes: the Principal Terms obligation is in supply licence condition (SLC) 7A. The 2022 decision tightened principal-terms disclosure (including brokerage costs) and required suppliers to use only brokers in a qualifying ADR scheme.
findings.evidence: CMS summary: the existing obligation to bring Principal Terms to the microbusiness's attention pre-contract is under SLC 7A.4, and the decision added a post-contract written requirement. Purely signposting Principal Terms during a sales call is not sufficient, and verbally agreed contracts require clear explanation of the Principal Terms. Brokerage costs must be shown via the Principal Terms as a total cost in pounds and pence over the contract duration, effective from 1 October 2022. A new supply licence condition requires suppliers to work only with brokers in a qualifying ADR scheme, effective from 1 December 2022. A proposed 1–14 day cooling-off period was not implemented. Ofgem's April 2024 press release (read earlier) later extended broker-fee display in principal terms to all non-domestic customers.
findings.limitations: These references come from a law-firm summary. The licence text itself was not read. The SLC reference for the termination-notice change is not stated on that page. The 2024 extension is described in the Ofgem press release as expected for contracts signed on and from 1 October 2024.

findings.claim: ESOS phase 4: qualification is assessed on 31 December 2026, and the compliance notification deadline is 5 December 2027. Phase 4 has stricter compliance routes and more action-plan reporting.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK ESOS guidance (DESNZ/Environment Agency, last updated 2 September 2026): ESOS is a mandatory energy assessment scheme for qualifying UK organisations, with an assessment every 4 years covering buildings, industrial processes and transport. "Your organisation qualifies for ESOS phase 4 if, on 31 December 2026, it meets the ESOS definition of a large undertaking." Corporate groups qualify if at least one UK group member is a large undertaking. The deadline for the phase 4 notification of compliance, submitted through MESOS, is 5 December 2027. For phase 3 the qualification date was 31 December 2022. Phase 4 changes: DECs and Green Deal assessments can no longer be used as alternative compliance routes. Progress against action plan commitments must be included, and unmet commitments explained. Compliance must use an energy audit or ISO 50001 certification (issued after 5 December 2023 and valid at 5 December 2027). A lead assessor must sign off unless total energy consumption is covered by ISO 50001 or is less than 40,000 kWh. Audit data must cover a 12-month period beginning no earlier than 6 December 2022, and audits must include site visits. A board-level director must sign off. Regulators may impose civil sanctions including financial penalties. Phase 3 participants must submit an annual progress update by 5 December 2026. The regulations were amended by the Energy Savings Opportunities Scheme (Amendment) Regulations 2026.
findings.limitations: The extract I read did not include the definition and thresholds of a 'large undertaking' (employee, turnover or balance sheet figures), which the page says are in section 1 of the phase 4 compliance guidance. I did not open that guidance. Check it before relying on the thresholds. ESOS is about energy assessment, not about contract choice.

findings.claim: The only current government energy-cost support found is the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme (BICS), a targeted scheme for eligible manufacturers. It is not a general support scheme for all business electricity buyers.
findings.evidence: GOV.UK press release (1 October 2026): applications opened for BICS, with eligible manufacturers urged to apply by 30 November to receive support from April 2027. Eligible businesses in England, Scotland and Wales will be exempt from paying the indirect costs of the Renewables Obligation, Feed-in Tariffs and Capacity Market. The release says BICS will cut manufacturers' electricity costs by up to 25 percent, and that the percentage discount depends on the underlying electricity price each company pays. It is aimed at more than 10,000 manufacturing businesses in the Modern Industrial Strategy's eight high-growth sectors and the foundational industries that supply them. Businesses confirmed as eligible and applying this year are also in line for an additional lump-sum payment equivalent to around a year's relief. The release also refers to extended support through the British Industry Supercharger for energy-intensive industries, and says the Northern Ireland Executive will receive funding for an equivalent scheme, subject to business case development. The earlier VAT Notice 701/19 (read in a previous task) describes the Energy Bill Relief Scheme as applying to energy use from 1 October 2022 up to and including 31 March 2023.
findings.limitations: The BICS source is a press release. Detailed eligibility criteria are in separate GOV.UK guidance for applicants that I did not read. No page I read names or describes a successor to the Energy Bill Discount Scheme, and I found no GOV.UK page stating whether a general successor exists. The VAT notice also mentions a temporary VAT zero rate for domestic supplies and other qualifying use, but I cannot confirm from it whether that covers ordinary business electricity.

notes:
T6: Not covered by any official page I opened: DUoS (distribution charges, set by DNOs under Ofgem price controls), the Feed-in Tariff, the CfD levy, the capacity market, and how suppliers pass non-commodity costs through to non-domestic customers by contract type. Page-open limits were used. Further tasks could target an Ofgem or DNO page on DUoS and a DESNZ or Low Carbon Contracts Company page on the CfD levy and capacity market. The NESO TNUoS data are forecasts for 2027/28, not final tariffs.
T7: Not found in pages I opened: the non-domestic switching timeline in Ofgem or Energy Ombudsman material (only Citizens Advice's 5 working days was read), a full list of grounds on which a supplier may object, the back-billing cap (the 12-month limit was seen only in search snippets and is not cited), and licence condition references for the termination-notice change. Page-open limits were used. A later step could open the Ofgem decision document or the licence conditions for exact references, and the Energy Ombudsman pages for back-billing.
T8: Gaps: (1) ESOS phase 4 'large undertaking' thresholds (employees, turnover, balance sheet) were not on the page extract I read, and the phase 4 compliance guidance was not opened. (2) No GOV.UK page confirmed whether a general successor to the Energy Bill Discount Scheme exists. BICS is a targeted manufacturing scheme, and BICS eligibility criteria come only from the press release. Page-open limit used.
